categories.description: Tools for fetching content from the outside world. Whenever 007 needs information that is not already on the local machine, this is where to start: fetch a web page, call an API, read a GitHub repository, search a platform, or render a page that only reveals its content after JavaScript runs. This category covers three ways to fetch. Real browsers — chrome-nosandbox, camoufox, lightpanda and Playwright — render pages, execute JavaScript, and get past bot checks such as Cloudflare Turnstile; they are the only option when a site refuses plain HTTP. Raw HTTP — curl plus jq — is the fastest and cheapest fetcher, ideal for static HTML and JSON APIs, but it needs full browser headers or the site may answer with a 40-byte empty shell or a challenge page. Platform entries — GitHub, YouTube, Bilibili, Douyin and others — give structured, read-only access to platform content (posts, videos, repositories, rankings) without writing a scraper, and their JSON output is ready for the agent to consume. The working order is: try curl first; if it returns nothing useful, switch to a browser; if the target is a known platform, prefer its dedicated entry. This category does not cover reading local files (see code and ops), searching a local codebase (see code), or recalling stored knowledge (see memory). It also does not write anything: every tool here is read-only by design, so fetching never mutates a remote service.

categories.name: Code
categories.description: Tools for working with source code: searching it, understanding it, reverse-engineering it, and auditing it. Whenever a task involves reading code, finding a function, understanding how a program works, decompiling a binary, or checking code for problems, start here. This category has three subcategories. Code search (ripgrep, codegraph) finds text and symbols in a codebase: ripgrep is the fast, .gitignore-aware text search for any string or pattern, while codegraph indexes a repository into symbols and a call graph for definition and reference queries — note that no index exists on 007 yet, so one must be built for the target repository before querying. Reverse engineering (Ghidra, rea) handles binaries and compiled programs with no source available: Ghidra is the local decompiler and disassembler, rea is the master CLI that orchestrates many reverse-engineering providers. Code audit (semgrep, run-audit.sh) scans source against rules to find vulnerability patterns and bad practices. This category does not cover fetching code from the internet (use the fetch platform entries), writing new code (the agent writes code with its own file tools, not through a registry entry), or security-specific scanning of dependencies and configurations (see security). If the question is 'what does this code do' or 'where is this in the codebase', the answer lives here.

categories.name: SEO
categories.description: Tools for analyzing and improving how a website performs in search engines and in AI-generated answers (SEO, GEO and AEO). Whenever a task asks how a site ranks, whether its pages are healthy for search, how good its content is, or what files help AI systems understand it, start here. This category has two subcategories. Content tools score and clean article text: quality scoring, AI-tone removal, and claim-and-citation checking, all reading plain txt, md or html. SEO tools audit whole pages and sites: the deterministic GEO/SEO/AEO auditor fetches one page and outputs JSON facts (booleans and counts, no invented total score), and the claude-seo skill library bundles 26 skills, 19 agents and 60 scripts for full SEO work. The /seo route ties them together: local audit output goes into a prompt and the model produces a fix package, quick in 180 seconds or deep in 420, and only --write touches source code. This category does not cover generic web fetching (see fetch), UI design (see design), or writing site content from scratch. If the task is 'make this site rank better' or 'check this site's SEO health', start here and let the auditor produce facts before the model proposes fixes.

categories.name: Design
categories.description: Tools for generating, checking, and improving visual design and user interfaces. Whenever a task involves creating an interface, checking a design against standards, verifying a page with your own eyes, or composing a video, start here. This category has three subcategories. UI generation produces interface layouts, design tokens and DESIGN.md specifications from a brand and a target, using the library of 84 real-site design documents as reference. Visual checking verifies designs: screenshot comparison through chrome-nosandbox or Playwright, and deterministic scoring through the impeccable anti-pattern detector, which runs fully offline and is the engine behind the /ui route. Video composition (hyperframes) builds videos from HTML with timing attributes and a GSAP timeline. A critical distinction lives here: the project's own DESIGN.md (a specification derived from its code) and the reference library's DESIGN.md files (analyses of other sites) share a name but must never be mixed, or the next audit gets polluted. This category does not cover SEO (see seo), fetching page content (see fetch), or media transcoding (see media). If the task is 'make this look good' or 'is this design correct', start here. The /ui and /design routes wrap these tools for chat use: /ui runs detect, aggregates rules, and produces a fix package, while /design applies a chosen style to a target project. Both routes are read-only unless --write is given explicitly.

categories.name: Security
categories.description: Tools for finding security vulnerabilities in code, dependencies and configurations. Whenever a task asks whether code is safe, whether secrets have leaked, or whether dependencies carry known CVEs, start here. This category has a single subcategory, scan, with five scanners. Bandit is the Python-only AST linter for dangerous patterns such as eval, subprocess with shell=True, and hardcoded passwords. Gitleaks scans code and history for leaked secrets using regex plus entropy, running fully offline. Pip-audit checks Python dependencies against the PyPI advisory database (OSV) for known CVEs. Trivy scans container images, filesystems and configs for CVEs and misconfigurations. Ast-grep searches and rewrites code by AST structure rather than regex, which makes it steadier than regex and lighter than semgrep; it is filed here because its structural matching is used for security-pattern scanning, though it is equally useful as a general code tool. The workflow is: scan first with the matching tool, then let the agent judge the findings, because scanners report candidates, not verdicts. This category does not cover general code search (see code), runtime environments (see runtime), or system administration (see ops). If the task is 'is this safe' or 'find the vulnerability', start here. Every scanner here runs locally; only semgrep fetches rules online, and only when no local rule snapshot exists on the host.

categories.name: Runtime
categories.description: Language runtimes and data-processing engines that other tools depend on. This category holds the interpreters and processors: Python 3.11, Node.js 22, jq for JSON, the Temurin JDK 25, npm and yarn for Node packages, and uv for Python tools. These are not tasks by themselves — they are the engines that run scripts and process data. The agent uses them implicitly whenever it needs to execute a Python script, parse JSON in a pipeline, run JavaScript, or install a command-line tool. Python is the base for the script layer and pip-installed tools; Node is the only runtime for the gateway, the Pi extensions and the frontend toolchain; the JDK exists because Ghidra requires it; jq is the default JSON slicer in shell pipelines; uv is the only installer for Python CLI tools and npm is the one for Node tools (yarn is installed but unused). This category does not include the scripts themselves (see ops), the applications built on these runtimes, or media processing (see media). If a task needs a particular language executed, confirm the runtime is here first. Version mismatches are the usual failure: if a tool complains about a missing runtime, check this category first before installing anything new, because duplicate runtimes cause more problems than they solve.

categories.name: Media
categories.description: Tools for processing documents and media files: converting formats, transforming images and video, extracting text, and generating speech. Whenever a task involves a file that is not plain text, start here. FFmpeg transcodes audio and video and extracts frames and audio tracks. ImageMagick converts, scales, crops and composites images. Tesseract OCR recognizes text inside images, most reliably on typeset text with --oem 1 --psm 6. Pandoc converts documents between markdown, HTML, docx, LaTeX and more, as a pure structural conversion. Mpv probes media files and extracts audio on this headless machine (there is no display for playback). Edge-tts turns text into speech through Microsoft Edge online TTS, producing mp3 files in 322 voices. These tools form a pipeline: extract with ffmpeg or mpv, read with tesseract, convert with pandoc or ImageMagick, speak with edge-tts. This category does not cover fetching media from the internet (see fetch), writing code (see code), or running language runtimes (see runtime). If the task is 'convert this file', 'read the text in this image', or 'turn this text into audio', start here. Output formats are the contract: ffmpeg writes mp4, mp3 or extracted frames; ImageMagick writes png, jpg or webp; pandoc writes md, html, docx or LaTeX; edge-tts writes mp3. Match the tool to the format you need.

categories.name: Operations
categories.description: Tools for operating and managing systems: containers, services, scripts, credentials and infrastructure. Whenever a task involves managing a server, running a container, executing a maintenance script, checking login state, or orchestrating a deployment, start here. This category has a single subcategory, ops-mgmt, with sixteen entries. It includes container management (docker-init documentation for the container bootstrap), GitHub authentication state (the gh CLI login persisted as a token file), the operations script library (capability drift checks, capability scans, CDP browser launchers, chrome-nosandbox wrappers, environment inventories, and the TOTP library), and the two skill SOPs for migration and forge. Several scripts still hardcode #3 paths such as /data/workspace and /data/cache; on 007 those sections are empty and only the portable sections apply, so read the notes before trusting a script's full output. Two entries are archived dead tools (lean-ctx and llmtrim) kept for reference, and one script (link-selftest) is #3-only and cannot run on 007. This category does not cover security scanning (see security), language runtimes (see runtime), or media processing (see media). If the task is 'run this maintenance job' or 'manage this server', start here. When a script fails, check its note first: most failures on 007 come from hardcoded #3 paths, not from missing tools.

categories.name: Memory
categories.description: Tools and documents describing the memory system: how 007 stores, recalls, and refines knowledge. This is a system category, not a callable tool category: none of its fourteen entries can be executed directly by the model. Instead, the agent loop calls Recall automatically every round to fetch relevant memories, and the memory system handles wiki pages, L1 logs and L3 refined knowledge in the background. The entries here document the four memory layers (fragments, candidates, long-term, structured), the wiki structure (entities, concepts, sources, synthesis), the recall mechanism (semantic, lexical and hybrid search), the write path (wiki_upsert_page for stable knowledge), and the five core skills (long-term library, adjudicator, retrieval, migration, forge) that govern how memory is kept and resolved. Two entries are duplicates under different names (cap-memory-recall-memory and ext-recall-memory share one implementation, as do the two wiki_upsert_page entries); use either, not both. One entry, the playbooks library, is a paper convention with no directory on disk and must not be relied on. This category exists for documentation and auditing, not for tool selection: when a task needs historical context or past experience, Recall handles it without the model picking a memory tool. The agent never picks a memory entry as a tool; Recall runs automatically, and the entries here only document the machinery.

subcategories.description: Scanning source code against rules to find problems. Semgrep runs static rules over source (vulnerability patterns, bad practices); it has no local rule snapshot on 007, so it fetches rules online by default and needs a prior download for offline scans. Run-audit.sh is the full audit entry: Cloudflare security-audit-skill plus Semgrep in two layers, local pre-screen then agent judgment. Use semgrep for a quick single scan and run-audit.sh for a complete audit. Semgrep version 1.182.1 was installed via pip; its rules come from the online registry by default because no local rule snapshot exists on 007. Run-audit.sh layers the Cloudflare security-audit-skill on top of semgrep: the local pass finds candidates, then the agent judges each one against the audit procedure. Use the script for a full audit and semgrep alone for a single file.

Analyzing binaries and compiled programs with no source available. Ghidra is the local reverse-engineering platform: decompile, disassemble and inspect, headless with JDK 25, no GUI needed. Rea is the master CLI that orchestrates many providers (175 commands): ghidra and jadx are ready, ida, hopper and kuna are missing. Use rea as the entry point for a reverse-engineering task and ghidra for a single decompile. Ghidra runs headless with JDK 25 and needs no GUI; its install lives at /data/tools/ghidra. Rea registers providers through environment variables and currently has ghidra and jadx ready, while ida, hopper and kuna are missing. For a quick answer about what a binary does, start with rea; for a deep decompile of one binary, go straight to ghidra.

Finding things in a codebase. Ripgrep is the fast text search: .gitignore-aware, multithreaded, and an order of magnitude faster than grep, ideal for any string or pattern. Codegraph indexes a repository into symbols and a call graph for definition, reference and dependency queries — but no index exists on 007 yet, so build one for the target repo before querying. Git answers history questions (what changed, who changed it, which commit introduced it) and is the only VCS here. Use this subcategory whenever the task is 'find this in the code'. Ripgrep respects .gitignore, so it skips vendored and generated files by default. Codegraph needs an index built for the target repository before it can answer queries; only /data/workspace/rea was ever indexed. When a search returns nothing, check whether the target is inside .gitignore or outside the indexed tree before concluding the code does not exist.

Generating interfaces and design specifications. These entries produce UI layouts, design tokens and DESIGN.md files from a brand and a target path, using the 84-file reference library as style input. The /design --write mode edits target source directly, but its backup relies entirely on a prompt sentence, so read-only mode is the default. The visual verification SOP (screenshots via chrome-nosandbox or Playwright) is filed here in the registry; for scored checks use the visual-check subcategory. The /design route takes a brand and a target path, feeds the reference library style into the model, and writes the result into the target project. The --write mode edits source directly and copies DESIGN.md into the project root, but its backup depends on a single prompt sentence, so prefer read-only runs and back up first. Keep the project's own DESIGN.md separate from the reference library at all times.

Composing videos from HTML source. Hyperframes writes composition, animation, title cards, subtitles, voiceover, audio-reactive visuals and transitions as HTML with data-* timing attributes plus a GSAP timeline, then lints, previews and renders with npx hyperframes. Note: it was never verified by actually running on #3, so treat the entry as provisional. The workflow is: write the video as HTML with data-* timing attributes, add a GSAP timeline for animation, then run npx hyperframes to lint, inspect, preview and render. Rendering runs on ffmpeg and edge-tts, both already in the registry. Because it was never run end-to-end on #3, verify the render step on a small sample before committing to a full video.

Verifying designs against rules and against your own eyes. The impeccable detector scores files and URLs for design anti-patterns fully offline and deterministically, and the /ui route scoring relies on it. The impeccable skill workflow documents 24 commands, but only detect is implemented. The gateway-timeouts entry documents a known timeout-truncation mechanism. Use this subcategory when the task is 'is this design correct'. The impeccable engine is the workhorse: it scores a file in 0.06 seconds and a URL in 2-29 seconds, fully offline, with zero API calls. The /ui route depends on it for all scoring. The skill workflow file documents 24 commands, but only detect has a real implementation, so do not invoke the others as CLI commands. The gateway-timeouts entry is documentation of a truncation mechanism, not a checker.

Real browser channels for pages that plain HTTP cannot read. Use these when a page needs JavaScript to render its content, or when Cloudflare Turnstile or another bot check blocks curl. Chrome-nosandbox is the general headless Chrome and the cheapest one-off dump; camoufox is the anti-detection browser that passes Turnstile; lightpanda is a lightweight JS engine that outputs markdown or HTML without rendering; Playwright automates all three kernels for interactive work and screenshots; scrapling adds TLS-fingerprint stealth to fetching. Browsers are slower and costlier than curl, so use them only when HTTP fetching fails. Camoufox is the one to reach for when Turnstile blocks everything else; it passed a live test against ping0.cc after the GTK3 and Firefox dependencies were installed. Playwright covers the automation case: scripted multi-step browsing, screenshots and traces, while chrome-nosandbox covers the one-off dump.

Low-level HTTP fetching and parsing. Curl fetches any URL and jq slices JSON; together they are the fastest and cheapest way to get content from the internet. Use this subcategory for static HTML pages and JSON APIs, and prefer it over browsers whenever the content is already in the response. Send full browser headers or the server may answer with an empty shell or a challenge page. The GitHub CLI and the httpx Python library live here too: gh for GitHub operations, httpx for HTTP calls inside Python scripts (with the environment proxy bypassed). The Tavily CLI is registered here but unusable without an API key.

Read-only entry points for specific platforms. These CLIs speak each platform's own interface and return structured JSON: agent-reach covers GitHub, YouTube, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Twitter, Reddit and more; yt-dlp reads video metadata, subtitles and downloads; the Bilibili client reads hot lists, rankings, search and creator pages. Use these when the target is a known platform, because structured output beats scraping HTML. For arbitrary websites, use the http or browser subcategories instead. Agent-reach is the broadest entry: one CLI covering GitHub, YouTube, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Twitter, Reddit, Xueqiu and BOSS, all output as JSON. Yt-dlp specializes in video metadata, subtitles and downloads. The Bilibili client covers hot lists, rankings, search and creator pages, but its minimal calls returned no data, so treat it as unverified.

Processing documents and media files. FFmpeg transcodes and extracts, ImageMagick converts and edits images, Tesseract reads text from images, Pandoc converts document formats, mpv probes media and extracts audio, edge-tts generates speech audio. Use this subcategory whenever the input or output is a non-text file. The pipeline order matters: extract media with ffmpeg or mpv first, read text with tesseract, convert documents with pandoc, edit images with ImageMagick, and generate speech with edge-tts last. Each tool handles one step; chaining them covers most document and media jobs without leaving the shell. When a file will not open, check its format first: the right tool depends on the input type, not on the task name.

Stable knowledge and its documentation. The wiki pages (entities, concepts, sources, synthesis), the extensions overview, the wiki lint tool, and the adjudicator skill live here. This is where durable, structured knowledge is kept and checked. The playbooks entry is a paper convention with no directory on disk. The wiki is the structured truth layer: entities record things, concepts record ideas, sources record where facts came from, and synthesis pages record conclusions. The extensions overview documents the 37 TypeScript extensions that register tools at session start. The adjudicator skill resolves conflicts between entries. Together these keep stored knowledge consistent and checkable.

The memory machinery itself: layers, recall, write path, and self-reporting. Recall is the unified lookup the agent loop calls every round; wiki_upsert_page writes stable knowledge; self-status, usage-report and detect-conflicts report on the system's own state. The long-term and retrieval skills govern storage and lookup. These are system mechanisms, not tools the model picks. Recall is the entry the agent loop calls every round, with hybrid search by default and semantic or lexical modes available. Wiki_upsert_page is the write path for stable knowledge. Self-status reports the agent's own state, usage-report shows which memories are used or dormant, and detect-conflicts surfaces contradictions for review. The long-term and retrieval skills govern storage rules and lookup order.

Operating and managing systems. Container bootstrap docs, GitHub login state, and the operations script library: capability drift and scan checks, CDP browser launchers, chrome-nosandbox wrappers, environment inventories, and the TOTP library. Also the migration and forge skill SOPs. Several scripts hardcode #3 paths, so read each entry's note before trusting its output. Two entries are archived dead tools and one script is #3-only. The script library covers capability drift checks, capability scans, CDP browser launchers, chrome-nosandbox wrappers, environment inventories, and the TOTP library. Two entries are archived dead tools (lean-ctx, llmtrim) kept for reference, and link-selftest is #3-only. The migration and forge skill SOPs are filed here because they govern deployment and tool-building operations.

Language runtimes and package managers. Python 3.11 runs scripts, Node 22 runs the gateway and JavaScript tools, the JDK 25 runs Ghidra, jq slices JSON, npm installs Node tools, uv installs Python tools, and yarn is installed but unused. These are engines, not tasks: the agent uses them implicitly. Confirm the needed runtime is here before running code in that language. Version notes: Python 3.11.2 is the system interpreter with no pyenv or conda; Node 22.23.4 is the only JavaScript runtime; the JDK is Temurin 25.0.5; jq is 1.6; npm is 10.9.9 and yarn is 1.22.22 classic. When a tool fails to start, check that its runtime is present here before reinstalling anything, since duplicate runtimes cause more failures than they fix.

Scanning for security vulnerabilities. Five scanners, each with a scope: bandit for Python source, gitleaks for leaked secrets in code and history, pip-audit for Python dependency CVEs, trivy for container and config CVEs and misconfigurations, ast-grep for structural pattern matching by AST. Scanners report candidates, not verdicts — the agent judges the findings. Use the scanner whose scope matches the target; for a full audit use the code/audit entry run-audit.sh. Each scanner has one scope, so pick by target: Python source goes to bandit, leaked secrets to gitleaks, Python dependencies to pip-audit, containers and configs to trivy, structural patterns to ast-grep. Run the matching scanner first, then judge the findings yourself: a scanner reports candidates, and only the agent decides whether a finding is a real vulnerability.

Scoring and cleaning article text. Three plain-text tools read txt, md or html from stdin or files: content_quality.py scores 0-100, content_humanize.py removes AI tone, content_verify.py checks claims and citation gaps. The 84-file DESIGN.md library is reference material for design language, and the TOOLKIT-INDEX.md is the routing table for the whole SEO toolchain (note: several of its entries are outdated). Use this subcategory when the task is about the quality of a piece of content. The three content tools accept txt, md or html through stdin or files and support --json output for agents. Content_quality.py returns a 0-100 score, content_humanize.py strips AI tone, content_verify.py finds claims without citations. The DESIGN.md library is reference material, not a spec, and the TOOLKIT-INDEX.md routing table has several outdated entries, so verify before following it blindly.

Auditing sites and running the SEO skill library. The deterministic GEO/SEO/AEO auditor fetches one page and outputs JSON facts with no invented total score. The claude-seo library bundles 26 skills, 19 agents and 60 scripts, though its setup and doctor steps report missing pieces on 007 (no .venv, no data directory). The llms.txt entry is a template and procedure only — no generator exists. The /seo route ties audit output to model-written fixes. Use this subcategory when the task is about a site's search performance. The claude-seo library is the largest entry here: 26 skills, 19 agents and 60 scripts, but its setup and doctor steps report missing pieces on 007 because there is no .venv and no data directory. The llms.txt entry has only a template and a checker; the file itself must be written by the model or by hand.
